channel.title: Robotics & AI Daily Briefing
channel.description: New cs.RO and cs.AI papers, bucketed and summarized every arXiv announcement day

item.title: The biggest manipulation gains today come from evolving the harness around a frozen model, while the papers that matter most for human-facing robots show policies that start moving when nobody asked, pick the wrong object in clutter, and change how people feel in ways that physical metrics miss.
item.description:
The biggest manipulation gains today come from evolving the harness around a frozen model, while the papers that matter most for human-facing robots show policies that start moving when nobody asked, pick the wrong object in clutter, and change how people feel in ways that physical metrics miss.
Several groups now improve robots without touching policy weights: a coding model rewrites the control harness, a teacher's harness is distilled into a 4B student, or lessons from past runs are stored as context. That makes the evaluation harness part of the product, and today's evaluation papers show how often cheap proxies (offline loss, a clean build, a module's name, a VLM judge) disagree with what actually runs. The behaviours those proxies miss are the ones people notice first: every tested VLA checkpoint moved on an empty instruction, generalists acted on the wrong object 30% of the time in clutter, and dual-encoder VLMs scored at chance on single-attribute changes. On the human side, an exosuit study and a dog-navigation pilot both show that what a robot does physically does not predict how it is perceived, so perception and choices have to be measured directly. Human data keeps getting cheaper to use, since action-free video, contact geometry and object motion carry most of the transfer, and humanoid motion generators are being closed around robot feedback so they can respond to people mid-motion.

item.title: A one-day week (only Monday's listing was published) in which the strongest work built structure around frozen policies, while a real-robot benchmark showed that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
item.description:
A one-day week (only Monday's listing was published) in which the strongest work built structure around frozen policies, while a real-robot benchmark showed that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
Monday 2026-10-12 was the only snapshot this week, so every trend below rests on a single listing and should be read as a signal rather than a confirmed pattern. It still continued the previous week's main thread: policies were improved from outside through revisable memory, failure monitors judged by the intervention they enable, and small adaptation modules on frozen weights. World-model ideas moved into training, so policies get supervision from predicted futures without paying for generation at deployment. Human demonstrations transferred as contacts, wrist-centred hand structure and latent actions rather than raw joint angles. For a team building robots that interact with people of different ages and cultures, the most relevant results were Spa-Bench, which shows VLAs losing spatial referents out of distribution, and JitterVLA, which gives a cheap way to check motion smoothness near people before a user study.

item.title: Robot policies are getting explicit structure around the frozen model (revisable memory, failure probes judged by what they let you fix, and human data transferred as contacts), while new benchmarks show that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
item.description:
Robot policies are getting explicit structure around the frozen model (revisable memory, failure probes judged by what they let you fix, and human data transferred as contacts), while new benchmarks show that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
Today's strongest manipulation results do not come from retraining the policy. Memory is being rebuilt as an auditable record with evidence links that can withdraw stale conclusions, and failure handling is judged by whether an alarm or probe leads to a useful intervention rather than by detection accuracy. World-model ideas are moving into training: predict the future to shape the policy's features, then skip or shrink that prediction at deployment. Human demonstrations transfer when they are expressed as contact goals, wrist-centred hand structure or latent actions rather than raw joint angles. On the human side, a real-robot benchmark finds VLAs execute the motions but lose spatial descriptions out of distribution, and interpretability work points to viewpoint transformation as the bottleneck, which is exactly what a robot needs when a person says "to my left". For a team building robots that talk with people of different ages and cultures, the practical move is to test spatial and perspective-dependent language explicitly, and to measure motion smoothness near people as its own outcome.

item.title: This week the useful robot work happened around the policy, not inside it: runtime layers on frozen VLAs, controls that deflate learned add-ons, and HRI tests showing that robots still miss what people actually say, point at and mean.
item.description:
This week the useful robot work happened around the policy, not inside it: runtime layers on frozen VLAs, controls that deflate learned add-ons, and HRI tests showing that robots still miss what people actually say, point at and mean.
Every day this week had a cluster about improving a frozen policy from outside (supervisors, trust gates, chunk-commitment rules, verified self-revision), and by Thursday the pattern was mature enough that a paired placebo study showed a scripted retreat can match a learned corrector. A second thread ran Tuesday, Thursday and Friday: VLAs reach high benchmark success while ignoring a swapped target, a synonym, a negation or a pointing gesture, which is the failure a robot talking to people of different ages and cultures will hit first. Human demonstrations were judged by what they fail to record (contacts, timing, pose accuracy) and transferred best through shared latent or contact-event representations. World models kept looking right while being wrong where a controller needs them, and the fixes favoured compact, control-relevant prediction targets and failure-aware training data. On the HRI side, social behaviour was treated as a set of planned channels (noise, gesture, face, speed), assistance was triggered by implicit human actions, and one cross-dataset study warned that cues validated at one site can reverse meaning at another.

item.title: Today's robot gains come from fixing what surrounds the policy (the state handed between skills, the checks before an action runs, and how human motion and intent are translated) rather than from bigger end-to-end models.
item.description:
Today's robot gains come from fixing what surrounds the policy (the state handed between skills, the checks before an action runs, and how human motion and intent are translated) rather than from bigger end-to-end models.
Across manipulation, navigation and humanoids, the papers with the clearest results leave the core policy mostly alone and work on its interfaces. Long-horizon chains break at skill seams because of the scene state one skill leaves for the next. Frozen VLAs are being wrapped with monitors, gates and residuals instead of being retrained. Navigation and manipulation harnesses keep large models for decisions and hand motion to dedicated tools. World-action models improve when they predict compact, control-relevant futures instead of pixels. Human demonstrations transfer when they are mapped into a shared latent or contact-event space. On the HRI side, pointing, handling, short intent-style instructions and negations all need explicit grounding, and cues that predict approach on one robot do not reliably carry over to another site. For a team building robots for people of different ages and cultures, the practical message is to instrument and test the interfaces (between skills, between model and actuator, between person and robot) at least as carefully as the policy itself.

item.title: Robots and the models around them keep believing they finished, understood or judged correctly when they did not, and today's working fixes are explicit check layers outside the model: rephrasing rules, verified counterfactual failures, deterministic scorers and sparse human edits.
item.description:
Robots and the models around them keep believing they finished, understood or judged correctly when they did not, and today's working fixes are explicit check layers outside the model: rephrasing rules, verified counterfactual failures, deterministic scorers and sparse human edits.
The same gap shows up across manipulation, agents, world models and HRI today. VLAs act as if a grasp happened, multimodal agents declare unfinished tasks done, world models predict success on verified failures, a one-word change of phrasing swings success by tens of points, and VLM verdicts about people and hazards track the prompt, the caption bank or the serving stack. The papers that report clear gains do not mainly scale the model. They add a layer that checks or reshapes what goes in and out: instruction rewriting rules, verified counterfactual failure data, an event table read by a deterministic scorer, verification gates before a self-revised skill or policy is adopted, and sparse mid-task human input that the robot integrates without replanning. For a team building robots for people of different ages and cultures, this points to auditing the interface between people and models as carefully as the policy itself.

item.title: Today's most useful results come from better controls and readouts, not bigger models: a scripted retreat matches a learned VLA corrector, reading logits beats a fine-tuned emotion model, and robots that read human actions help about as well as robots that are told what to do.
item.description:
Today's most useful results come from better controls and readouts, not bigger models: a scripted retreat matches a learned VLA corrector, reading logits beats a fine-tuned emotion model, and robots that read human actions help about as well as robots that are told what to do.
Several papers today show that how something is measured or read out changes the conclusion more than the model does: a paired placebo shrinks the value of a learned VLA corrector, a logit readout turns 'VLMs fail at fine-grained emotion' into 'VLMs beat the fine-tuned model', and a compact policy matches systems 40-160x larger once its visual encoder is controlled. On the HRI side, assistance is increasingly triggered by what the person does (an action's outcome, a hand pose, a push on a carried load) rather than by an explicit instruction, while LLM-driven robots become easier to supervise when their plans are exposed as typed, structured commitments. In manipulation, contact feedback is being added to vision-first policies through the cheapest available channel, and a growing runtime layer decides how much of a frozen policy's action chunk to trust. World models keep showing the same gap: video that looks right while actions, hidden objects or unstable modes are wrong. For a team building interactive robots, the common thread is to test the specific property you rely on (the human cue, the contact event, the occluded object) with a control condition, before adding learned machinery.

item.title: Social robots are starting to plan how loud, fast and expressive they are, while new probes show VLAs often ignore what the person actually asked.
item.description:
Social robots are starting to plan how loud, fast and expressive they are, while new probes show VLAs often ignore what the person actually asked.
Several papers today treat social behaviour as something the robot actively produces: footstep noise, gesture timing, facial expression and execution speed are planned outputs, not side effects. A second group treats the human as a physical partner with their own forces, fatigue and fragility rather than as an obstacle or a remote operator. At the same time, diagnostic work on VLAs shows that nominal task success hides weak instruction following: policies grab the object the scene suggests, and safety refusals learned in text do not carry over to actions or grounding outputs. The practical consequence for an HRI team is that interaction quality has to be measured channel by channel, and that 'does the robot do what this person asked, and refuse what it should' needs its own tests. Much of the remaining engineering work fixes frozen policies at execution time, which is where a deployment team can act today.
